nameStory: Micractinium gets its name from Greek words meaning 'small ray,' referring to how these tiny cells arrange themselves in star-like clusters that look like microscopic sunbursts. The species name 'pusillum' means 'very small' in Latin, which is quite fitting since you'd need a magnifying glass or microscope to see individual colonies clearly!
description: Micractinium pusillum is a microscopic freshwater green algae that forms tiny, floating colonies in ponds and lakes. Each colony looks like a miniature green star or snowflake, made up of just a few cells arranged in a radial pattern. Individual colonies are barely visible to the naked eye, appearing as tiny green specks in the water, but they can sometimes form larger, more noticeable green patches when conditions are right. This is one of nature's smallest 'plants' that you might actually spot during a pond exploration.

idTips.label: Colony shape
idTips.description: Look for tiny star-shaped or cross-shaped green clusters floating in still water - they look like microscopic green snowflakes

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual colonies are almost too small to see clearly with the naked eye, appearing as tiny green dots smaller than a pinhead

idTips.label: Water appearance
idTips.description: When abundant, creates a faint greenish tinge to pond water that looks dusty or powdery rather than slimy

idTips.label: Cell arrangement
idTips.description: With magnification, you can see 4-8 round cells arranged like spokes of a wheel, each cell bright emerald green

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Colonies drift freely in the water without any swimming motion - they're completely at the mercy of currents

habitat: Found in quiet freshwater environments like small ponds, shallow lake edges, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Prefers nutrient-rich waters where it can float freely in the upper water column where sunlight penetrates. Often discovered in temporary pools, woodland ponds, and the calm backwaters of larger water bodies.

seasonality.spring: Begins appearing in warming waters as ice melts, often creating the first subtle green tinge in previously clear winter ponds.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance during warm months when you're most likely to notice the faint green coloration it adds to pond water.
seasonality.fall: Numbers decline as temperatures drop, though colonies may persist in protected, sun-warmed shallows until first frost.
seasonality.winter: Largely absent from the water column, surviving as dormant cells in pond sediments until spring warming begins.

funFact: Despite being one of the tiniest organisms you might spot in a New England pond, Micractinium colonies can actually help scientists determine water quality - their presence often indicates clean, well-oxygenated water that's healthy for fish and other aquatic life!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other microscopic green algae that create greenish water, but Micractinium's star-shaped colonies are distinctive under magnification. Unlike stringy algae that form long threads, or sheet-like algae that create surface films, Micractinium creates that 'dusty green' look to water rather than obvious slime or mats.
contextualKnowledge: While called an 'algae,' Micractinium is actually more closely related to land plants than to seaweeds - it's part of the green plant lineage that eventually gave rise to mosses, ferns, and flowering plants. Many people don't realize that these tiny pond organisms are actually distant cousins of the trees and flowers around them!
compareHints: Micractinium pusillum differs from its relative M. bornhemiense primarily in colony size and cell number - pusillum tends to have smaller colonies with fewer cells per star-shaped cluster. Both create similar star patterns, but pusillum's colonies are more delicate and typically have 4-6 cells rather than the 6-8 cells often seen in bornhemiense. In the field, this difference is nearly impossible to detect without magnification.
